author: @zeeshangla

text: Your definition of controllability is actually reachability, in continuous systems they are equivalent but for discrete systems they are not. To be reachable the system must be able to go from your initial state to any other state, to be controllable the system must be able to go from any initial state to zero. In discrete systems it is easy to see that a A = [0 0; 0 0] would be controllable (gets to zero from any point in one sampling without depending on B), but it would only be reachable if B = [1 0; 0 1] (individually control each state). Great video nonetheless.

text: Unfortunately, I don't remember the Jordan Form approach from my university days forever ago and haven't used it since! So, I don't have a great answer (maybe someone reading this comment can chime in). I quickly asked ChatGPT your question and got a long response, but here is the main takeaway: [If you have two 1x1 blocks, each controllable, the system as a whole is controllable. Each block individually has index 1, but for the system as a whole, you need two steps to reach any state (since you have two independent modes). For diagonalizable systems of dimension, n, all 1x1 Jordan blocks, then index is n if all modes are controllable.] Sorry I'm not more help here!
